new_paragraphs: The articles fall into four groups. Cost pieces break down what you pay and why, from a private chef at home to a plated wedding. Comparison pieces put two options side by side — private chef against restaurant, grazing table against buffet, full service against drop-off — so you can see which one fits your evening. Menu and idea pieces give you formats that work in Dubai's climate and venues. Timing pieces cover how far ahead to book and how the seasons move demand.

new_paragraphs: Send your date, guest count and venue — your catering blog proposal arrives.
Book catering blog about 2 weeks ahead off-peak, and 6 weeks ahead between November and March.
Confirm the catering blog menu roughly 7 days before, once your numbers settle.
Ask about dietary covers for catering blog when you enquire, not inside the final 48 hours .

add_block.new_heading: How we decide what goes in an article
new_paragraphs: An article gets written when hosts keep asking the same question and the honest answer takes more than a sentence. That is why the library leans toward costs, comparisons and timing instead of trend pieces. Every price quoted is a rate published on this site, so an article and a service page not disagree. Where a claim is regulatory — VAT, food safety, licensing — it carries a link to the source, because a reader planning a wedding should be able to verify a rule without taking a caterer's word for it.

What you will not find is invented statistics. Where a pattern comes from our own bookings instead of published research, the article says so plainly. The 2026 trends piece is labelled first-party observation for exactly that reason, and it carries no percentages, because attaching numbers would have meant inventing them.

new_paragraphs: Catering prices move on three levers, and every cost article is built around them. The menu sets the ingredient floor. The service level sets the labour, which is the largest line on most quotes — a drop-off tray needs almost no staff, a plated dinner needs a brigade. The guest count spreads the fixed costs, which is why a dinner for eight can cost more per head than a reception for eighty.

Read any article's key facts first: they carry the numbers and the lead times in one block. Then compare against your own brief instead of against another caterer's headline figure, because two quotes are only comparable when they cover the same inclusions. If a quote omits staffing, rentals or the 5% VAT line, it is not cheaper — it is incomplete.

add_block.new_heading: Seasonality changes what you should read
new_paragraphs: Dubai's calendar splits the year. From November to March the outdoor season runs, nights sit near 19°C, and weddings, galas and the conference circuit compete for the same weekends. Between May and September, indoor planning dominates and the articles on villa and apartment dining matter more than the terrace and yacht pieces.

Ramadan moves each year and reshapes service entirely, because iftar is timed to sunset instead of to a convenient hour. If your event falls in that month, the iftar and suhoor articles cover the timing, the staffing and the menu pattern that follow from it.

new_paragraphs: Figures and rules referenced across these pages come from official sources: the UAE Ministry of Finance (5% VAT on catering, in force since 1 January 2018), Dubai Municipality (Food Code, including requirements for food transportation and delivery vehicles and mandatory food-handler training), and Weather and Climate (Dubai December averages of 27°C by day and 19°C at night). Confirm current requirements before you book.

new_paragraphs: How much does a private chef cost in Dubai?
Most private-chef dinners run about AED 700 to 950 per person, moving toward the upper end for a small table. The full breakdown is in the private chef cost article.
Are the prices in these articles real?
Yes. Every figure is a rate published on this site, not an estimate. Where an article states a rule or a statistic, it cites an official UAE source.
How far ahead should I book?
Two to three weeks off-peak, and six to eight weeks or more between November and March when the season is busiest.
Do you cover Ramadan and festive periods?
Yes, with dedicated pieces on iftar at home, suhoor, Ramadan trends, Christmas and New Year, because each has its own timing and menu pattern.
